newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Buoyant UK consumers to boost April sales.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Buoyant UK consumers to boost April sales.

text.p: UK retail sales are set to show an increase in April as an income tax cut and windfall payment boosted already-buoyant consumer spending, analysts said. "The pace of spending on the high street is looking increasingly robust as consumer sentiment continues to improve," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "Most of the signs are pointing to fairly buoyant sales again this month."
A Reuters poll of economists produced a consensus forecast for a 0.3 percent rise in sales over the month of April, taking the year-on-year growth rate to 4.1 percent from 4.0 previously.
The figures are due at 0830 GMT on Thursday.
Analysts pointed to the Confederation of British Industry's latest distributive trades survey which showed April sales volumes at their highest level since November last year.
The survey found a positive balance of 42 percent of retailers reported a rise in sales, up from 33 percent in March.
Robust growth in weekly sales figures from the John Lewis Partnership -- a leading department store group -- was further evidence of improving consumer sentiment, they said.

One reason to expect a strong sales report is the boost to consumers' bank balances, not only from a one penny income tax cut, announced in November which finally fed through last month, but also from Alliance & Leicester windfall payments.

The building society gave millions of shares to its members last month as it converted into a bank. A whole host of societies are set to follow suit this summer, flooding with the economy with more than 20 billion pounds in windfall payments.

"Beneficial influences on consumer spending during the month will have been the windfall arising from the Alliance & Leicester float and the tax cuts from last November's Budget," David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said.
But the extent of the impact is difficult to decipher.
"It is still uncertain how big a percentage of those windfall gains consumers will be spending," said David at HSBC.
She said evidence of strong saving in the first quarter of the year suggested people were putting away their windfall gains rather than spending them.
"Our own forecast includes spending of about 10 to 30 percent of those windfall gains at the moment and the trend that retail sales are seeing at the moment is consistent with that forecast."

Uncertainty as to the outcome of the May 1 general election could have been one of the few factors to have worked against the general growth in sales last month. "Perhaps consumers were hanging onto their cash until they were certain what the outcome was for the rest of the year," said David.

David Smith, economist at Williams de Broe, said an unusually early Easter holiday could also have distorted the picture. But he forecast a 0.4 percent monthly rise, leaving sales 4.0 percent higher year-on-year.

Strong sales in April last year mean year-on-year growth will look fairly flat but that belies bubbling consumer spending. And to ease fears on the inflation front, economists said low producer price costs are reducing the temptation for retailers to raise prices. Furthermore, consumers are still showing signs of price discrimination, lapping up cut price offers but baulking at higher prices.
